THOUSAND OAKS, CALIFORNIA - MAY 17: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters on May 17, 2023 in Thousand Oaks, California. The Federal Trade Commission is suing to block the drugmaker from acquiring the smaller pharmaceutical company Horizon Therapeutics for $27.8 billion.
Mario Tama/Getty Images
When regulators at the European Medicines Agency published the full scientific rationale behind Europe's withdrawal of avacopan on August 6, 2026, they put on record something that clinical trial sponsors and drug regulators worldwide will be studying for years: a step-by-step account of how nine altered patient records — changed after a trial's database was sealed and treatment assignments were revealed — can destroy the evidentiary foundation of a $459 million drug approval. The
EMA's Article 20 Public Assessment Report
, published August 6, 2026, documents the sequence in full.
The assessment report, which explains the grounds for the European Commission's August 6 formal revocation of avacopan (Tavneos) across all EU member states and the European Economic Area, is the most detailed regulatory accounting yet of what the New England Journal of Medicine called, in its June 29 retraction of the ADVOCATE trial,
conduct "inconsistent with proper research conduct."
The
EMA CHMP recommended revocation
on June 25, 2026.
For patients and clinicians in the United States, where Tavneos remains FDA-approved and available while the agency evaluates Amgen's July 23 formal hearing submission, the EMA's published reasoning is not just European history. The same data-integrity failure that ended avacopan's four-year European run is the basis for the
FDA's own proposal to withdraw Tavneos
, issued April 27, 2026 — and the EMA's documented conclusion that a company-sponsored independent re-analysis cannot repair a GCP violation may preview exactly where the US hearing is heading.
What "Database Lock" Means — and Why Breaking It Matters
To understand what went wrong in the ADVOCATE trial, the pivotal Phase 3 study that supported avacopan's approval in both the US and EU, it helps to understand one of clinical research's most important procedural safeguards.
In a blinded randomized trial, a database lock is the point at which data collection is formally declared complete. Access to the data is sealed, no further changes are permitted without a formal documented amendment, and — critically — unblinding occurs only after the lock. The sequence exists for a specific reason: if anyone with knowledge of which patients received the experimental drug, rather than the control, can alter patient outcome assessments, the results of the trial can be biased. Whether that bias is conscious or unconscious is irrelevant to its regulatory impact. The standard is structural: the data must be collected and recorded by people who did not know which treatment each patient received. This requirement is codified in the
ICH E6 Good Clinical Practice guidelines
, the international standard governing clinical trial conduct.
In the ADVOCATE trial, according to the EMA's published assessment report and the
FDA's April 27 NOOH letter
, that sequence was violated in a specific and consequential way.
What the EMA Found Happened in November 2019
The ADVOCATE trial enrolled 331 patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) or microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) — the two main forms of ANCA-associated vasculitis, rare autoimmune conditions in which the immune system attacks small blood vessels, causing organ damage that can be fatal without aggressive treatment. The
ADVOCATE trial registration record
(NCT02994927) compared avacopan against a standard high-dose corticosteroid taper, both combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
Avacopan works by blocking the C5a receptor (C5aR1) on neutrophils, disrupting a self-amplifying inflammatory loop that is central to ANCA vasculitis pathology. When ANCA antibodies activate neutrophils, those neutrophils release factors that activate the complement system's alternative pathway, generating C5a — a potent inflammatory mediator. C5a then primes more neutrophils for ANCA-driven activation, sustaining the cycle of vascular damage. Blocking C5aR1 with avacopan interrupts this loop while theoretically allowing corticosteroid dose reduction. The underlying
C5a receptor pathway in ANCA vasculitis
has been studied extensively.
According to the EMA's published assessment report, after the first database lock on November 5, 2019, sponsor personnel with access to the unblinded data identified that the ADVOCATE trial had not met one of its most important findings: superiority at week 52 for sustained remission. Nine patients were then selected for re-adjudication of their primary endpoint assessments — meaning that independent committee members were asked to reassess whether those patients were in sustained remission or not. At week 52, five of those nine patients changed status. All five were in the avacopan group; all five moved from "not in sustained remission" to "sustained remission." The
EMA assessment report
and a
Vasculitis International summary
both document this sequence in detail.
The FDA's investigation, triggered by an independent expert report produced for a shareholder lawsuit and later confirmed by Amgen's own response to FDA information requests, identified two ChemoCentryx employees who had access to unblinded data and were involved in this process: Huibin Yue, PhD, the company's director of biostatistics, and Pirow Bekker, MD, PhD, who served as ChemoCentryx's chief medical officer and is listed as a co-author of the original ADVOCATE trial paper published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
Healio's coverage of FDA findings
covers these specific findings.
None of this appeared in the NDA submission or in the 2021 NEJM publication. The academic leaders of the trial — Dr. David Jayne of Cambridge and Dr. Peter Merkel of the University of Pennsylvania — were unaware it had occurred. When they learned of it through the FDA investigation, they requested the retraction. The
NEJM retraction notice
, published June 29, 2026, describes the conduct as "inconsistent with proper research conduct."
Why Amgen's Independent Re-Analysis Couldn't Save the Drug in Europe
After the data manipulation came to light, Amgen commissioned the Duke Clinical Research Institute (DCRI) to conduct a fully blinded independent re-adjudication of the ADVOCATE primary endpoints — an attempt to answer the question of whether the original trial conclusions hold even when the altered records are properly re-examined by an external party. Amgen's
FAQ on the TAVNEOS regulatory update
outlines the company's rationale for commissioning the re-adjudication.
The DCRI re-adjudication confirmed noninferiority of avacopan versus the prednisone taper for remission at week 26 — 68.1% versus 67.1%, a difference of 2.2 percentage points — and for sustained remission at week 52, 61.4% versus 52.4%, a 9.8 percentage point difference. These figures are broadly consistent with the original trial results and suggest avacopan has a real treatment effect. Amgen's
July 23, 2026 FDA hearing submission
presents the full re-adjudication data.
But the DCRI re-adjudication did not reproduce the original superiority finding at week 52. The original ADVOCATE analysis had reported a 12.5 percentage point superiority (95% CI, 2.6% to 22.3%) — a statistically significant result. The DCRI re-adjudication produced a 9.8 percentage point difference (95% CI, -0.3 to 19.9) — not statistically significant. The superiority claim was the centerpiece of avacopan's marketing value and much of its clinical rationale: not just matching steroids, but outperforming them in sustained remission.
The EMA's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) considered the DCRI re-adjudication and rejected it as a remedy. This is the key regulatory finding that US readers tracking the FDA hearing need to understand. Once a clinical trial's database has been locked and treatment assignments unblinded, any subsequent re-adjudication of primary endpoints — even by an entirely independent external party — cannot restore GCP compliance to the original data, because the contamination of the data environment is structural and irreversible. The DCRI worked from a data context that had already been shaped by unblinded sponsor personnel. No new analysis, however carefully blinded, can retroactively undo that. The
EMA assessment report
explains this structural reasoning explicitly.
The CHMP's conclusion, adopted June 25, 2026: the ADVOCATE study was conducted in breach of Good Clinical Practice principles, the data cannot be relied upon to demonstrate Tavneos's effectiveness, and post-marketing data and post-hoc analyses are insufficient to fill that evidentiary gap. The
EMA announcement of this recommendation
was published June 26, 2026.
A Parallel Safety Signal — and Its Independent Weight
While the GCP violation is the primary driver of both European and US regulatory action, a parallel pharmacovigilance crisis has deepened the case against avacopan and may independently shift the benefit-risk balance even if Amgen were to rehabilitate the efficacy evidence.
In its March 31, 2026
FDA drug safety communication
, the FDA identified 76 cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with reasonable evidence of causal association with avacopan — 74 serious outcomes, 54 hospitalizations, and 8 deaths in the global dataset.
The most acute picture is in Japan. Kissei Pharmaceutical disclosed in May 2026 that 20 patients had died after taking Tavneos in Japan since the drug went on sale in 2022, including 13 deaths among 22 cases of vanishing bile duct syndrome — a condition in which the small bile ducts inside the liver are progressively destroyed, impairing bile flow and potentially causing cirrhosis and liver failure. Amgen's
statement on the Japanese VBDS data
notes that "these figures include cases for which a causal relationship with the product could not be determined."
Amgen has noted that as of its July 23 submission, no confirmed VBDS deaths have been attributed to Tavneos among the more than 8,000 patients treated in the United States. The company updated US prescribing information on May 29, 2026, adding stronger liver monitoring requirements. Amgen's
FAQ on TAVNEOS
provides current prescribing guidance.
The EMA's Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) had already moved to reinforce liver monitoring requirements in Europe before the full revocation. The CHMP's revocation rationale explicitly relied on both the data integrity failure and the hepatotoxicity risk: with the sole pivotal trial unusable and post-marketing evidence insufficient to replace it, the serious liver risks are no longer outweighed by a proven benefit.
A Precedent for Every Drug Approved on a Single Pivotal Trial
The Tavneos case is being closely watched across the pharmaceutical industry precisely because of what it establishes about the limits of post-approval remediation.
Most major drug approvals rest on at least two adequate and well-controlled trials. The FDA and EMA occasionally permit approval on the basis of a single pivotal study — as they did with avacopan, in part because ANCA-associated vasculitis is rare and conducting two large trials would be extremely difficult — but this pathway leaves the approval more exposed if that single study is subsequently compromised. The
FDA's Notice of Opportunity for Hearing
addresses the evidentiary standards that apply in this context.
The EMA has now established that a post-approval Good Clinical Practice finding that invalidates the sole pivotal study is sufficient grounds for EU revocation — without requiring a concurrent catastrophic new safety signal to drive the decision. A drug can be pulled from the European market solely because the data that justified its approval can no longer be trusted, even if post-marketing real-world evidence and a company-commissioned independent re-analysis suggest it probably works. Regulatory standards for evidentiary integrity are not simply a proxy for clinical benefit; they are an independent requirement.
Sponsors holding EU authorizations supported by a single pivotal study now face a direct and documented precedent. Any post-approval GCP finding that invalidates the pivotal data can trigger revocation, and neither the drug's apparent real-world effectiveness nor a company-funded re-adjudication provides a reliable defense.
Amgen Contests the US Withdrawal — and the FDA Hearing Is Still Live
In the United States, the story is not over. Tavneos remains FDA-approved and commercially available, with US sales of $119 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a 32% year-over-year increase — according to
Amgen's Q1 2026 financial results
.
On July 23, 2026, Amgen formally submitted its package in support of a public hearing, contesting the FDA's April 27 withdrawal proposal. The
Amgen FDA hearing submission
includes the DCRI re-adjudication results, a systematic literature review and meta-analysis covering 71 real-world studies involving more than 2,200 patients (remission rates of 87% at six months and 93% at 12 months), post-marketing safety data, and patient and clinician testimonials.
Amgen's legal position is that the FDA's withdrawal proposal rests on a disputed characterization of the 2019 re-adjudication process, that the ADVOCATE trial as a whole still constitutes adequate and well-controlled evidence of effectiveness under the relevant statutory standard, and that the DCRI's fully blinded independent re-adjudication represents a sufficient remediation of the identified concerns.
The CHMP considered essentially the same argument and rejected it. Whether the FDA takes the same view — or whether the US statutory framework and the specific evidence Amgen has marshaled will yield a different outcome — is the regulatory question that will determine whether avacopan survives in any major market.
For US patients with GPA or MPA currently taking Tavneos, the practical answer for now remains what it has been since April: the drug is available, the FDA is in an active review, and any decisions about treatment should be made with a treating physician who has reviewed the agency's safety communications, particularly regarding liver function monitoring. The
FDA March 31 safety communication
is the appropriate guide on hepatic risk for patients currently on the drug.
The patient community's position on what is at stake was stated clearly by Vasculitis International after the CHMP recommendation: avacopan
addressed "a specific and underappreciated burden"
— the impact of glucocorticosteroids on patients' daily lives — and removing it leaves clinicians without a tool specifically designed to reduce that burden.
The FDA's decision on Amgen's hearing request will determine whether that burden remains addressed in the US, or whether European patients and American patients will share the same outcome.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is Tavneos (avacopan) still available in the United States?
Yes. As of August 14, 2026, Tavneos remains FDA-approved and available to US patients. The FDA has proposed withdrawal, but that proposal does not take effect until the agency completes its formal hearing process. Amgen submitted its defense package on July 23, and the FDA Commissioner will determine whether to hold a public hearing and then issue a final decision. Until that decision is made, no change in Tavneos's US approval status has occurred. Patients should discuss the current situation with their physician and follow FDA guidance on liver function monitoring, updated May 29, 2026. The
FDA CDER Tavneos withdrawal proposal page
provides the most current official status.
Why did Europe pull avacopan if clinical re-analysis showed the drug still works?
The EMA's revocation is not a finding that avacopan is ineffective — it is a finding that the evidence for its effectiveness can no longer be trusted, because the pivotal trial was conducted in violation of Good Clinical Practice standards. The committee found that once trial data have been altered by unblinded sponsor personnel after the database is locked, no subsequent re-analysis can retroactively make those data reliable under GCP. The DCRI re-adjudication produced results consistent with the original trial, but it was commissioned by Amgen and performed in a data environment already shaped by the original manipulation. The structural problem — GCP violation, not clinical failure — is why real-world evidence and company-funded re-analysis were not accepted as substitutes for an intact pivotal trial. The
EMA's full assessment report
sets out this reasoning in detail.
What specifically happened to the ADVOCATE trial data?
After the trial's database was locked on November 5, 2019, and treatment assignments were unblinded, ChemoCentryx personnel with access to unblinded data identified nine patients for re-adjudication of their primary endpoint assessments. Five of those nine patients were in the avacopan arm; all five had their status changed from "not in sustained remission" to "sustained remission." Those five reclassifications converted a non-superior outcome at week 52 into the superiority finding that became central to the drug's regulatory approval and marketing. The academic leads of the trial — Drs. David Jayne and Peter Merkel — were not told this had occurred. When FDA investigators uncovered it years later, Jayne and Merkel requested that the NEJM retract the 2021 paper.
The NEJM retracted the paper
on June 29, 2026.
Healio's detailed FDA investigation report
covers the specific conduct the FDA's investigation identified.
What are the liver risks US patients should know about?
The
FDA's March 2026 liver injury communication
identified 76 cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with reasonable evidence of causal association to avacopan — 74 serious outcomes and 8 deaths globally. Some cases involved vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS), a condition in which the bile ducts inside the liver are progressively destroyed; VBDS can cause permanent liver damage and has been fatal. In Japan, Kissei Pharmaceutical reported 20 deaths among Tavneos patients since 2022, including 13 among 22 documented VBDS cases. No confirmed VBDS deaths have been attributed to US patients as of Amgen's July 23 filing. The US prescribing information was updated May 29, 2026, to require liver function monitoring before treatment initiation and at regular intervals during treatment. Patients and clinicians should review those monitoring requirements with particular attention to the first three months of treatment, when the risk appears highest.

Cybin Inc., doing business as

for major depressive disorder has FDA
Breakthrough Therapy Designation
and is in a three-study Phase 3 program (APPROACH, EMBRACE, EXTEND), with APPROACH enrollment completed and topline data targeted for Q4 2026. IM NSA

has completed a Phase 2 study in generalized anxiety disorder showing clinically meaningful reductions in anxiety and short in-clinic treatment times, with next-study design expected by Q3 2026. Preclinical
HLP005
phenethylamine/tryptamine derivatives are advancing toward a potential development candidate in the second half of 2027. Helus Pharma details planned and actual use of approximately
$164.3M
of October 2025 financing proceeds, heavily focused on HLP003 Phase 3 trials and working capital, and discloses ongoing negative operating cash flow and the need for additional capital. The company highlights an extensive IP estate with over
125 granted patents
and hundreds of pending applications worldwide.
Positive
HLP003 granted FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation
, providing access to expedited review and enhanced FDA guidance that may shorten development timelines.
Phase 2a and durability data for HLP003
show large, statistically significant and sustained MADRS score improvements in MDD with high remission rates up to 12 months.
HLP004 Phase 2 GAD trial
demonstrated clinically meaningful HAM-A improvements and a well-tolerated, ~90-minute treatment window compatible with existing clinic workflows.
The company has built a large IP portfolio with
28 U.S. and 97 non-U.S. granted patents
plus extensive pending applications, supporting long-term exclusivity.
Negative
The company reports
negative cash flow from operating activities
and states it will need additional equity, debt, or partnerships, with no assurance such financing will be available.
Multiple programs and milestones, including
Phase 3 HLP003 and HLP005 candidate selection
, depend on timely capital access and successful clinical execution, adding development risk.

EXCLUSIVE: Drug companies choosing not to sell life-saving and life-extending medicines in Canada
While some drugs used to treat rare diseases have been approved by Health Canada, they're not always made available to Canadians. Cristina Howorun reports on the challenges some Canadians battling uncommon illnesses continue to face.
By Cristina Howorun
Posted August 14, 2026 2:03 pm.
Last Updated August 14, 2026 7:21 pm.
When Ruchi Ambike found out that Novartis got Health Canada approval for Vanrafia she was ecstatic. The drug can possibly slow down the progression of her Immunoglobulin gA nephropathy, (IgAN) and ultimately, end-stage kidney disease.
“It’s exciting because we have no IgAN drugs in Canada,” she says from her Mississauga home.
IgAN is a rare autoimmune disorder affecting the kidneys, limiting their ability to filter waste properly. Some patients progress to end-stage kidney disease which means a life on dialysis or a kidney transplant. There is no cure for IgAN and no cure for kidney disease – which impacts one in 10 Canadians.
“There are six FDA-approved medications specifically for igAN in the States and two more on the way this year,” Ambike explains, none of which are available in Canada.
Novartis issued a
media release
celebrating its Health Canada approval, but just weeks later CityNews learned the drug wouldn’t be making it to pharmacies in the country because Novartis decided not to continue with the approval process for Canadian patients.
In a statement to CityNews, a spokesperson writes: “While Novartis remains committed to expanding access to our medicines for patients in Canada, we have determined that under the current Canadian access environment, the likelihood of successfully securing reimbursement for Vanrafia is limited. As such, Novartis Canada has made the decision not to seek reimbursement for Vanrafia in IgAN at this time.”
“The unfortunate thing is this is not the first time this has happened,” says Dr. Michelle Hladunewich, a nephologist and the Physician in Chief at the Department of Medicine at Sunnybrook Health Sciences.
“It doesn’t sit well with me as a physician or as somebody who participated in the trial, but it seems to be the way its happening lately, especially with new drugs in Canada.”
“
Canadians have only access to 18 per cent of all innovative medicines that are available around the world. Americans have access to over 90 per cent,” explains Dr. Bettina Hamelin, President and CEO of Innovative Medicines Canada, which represents Canadian pharmaceutical companies.
“Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, which are the richer countries in this world, have access to about 28 per cent [of innovative medicines],” Hamelin says from her Toronto office, explaining that the big problems are time and money.
“Right now, Canadians wait an average of two and half years before they can access innovative medicines,” Hamelin explains.
Drug companies have to follow a complex sequential process after getting Health Canada approval before making it into patient’s medicine cabinets.
After a drug is approved by Health Canada, the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board sets a drug ceiling – the most a drug can cost – by comparing prices with other OECD countries. Then the Canada Drug Agency (CDA) makes a recommendation on cost and if the drug should be covered by federal and/or provincial health plans. The Pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance begins to negotiate drug prices on behalf of the entire country, and then provinces have to determine whether or not they can afford to list the drug on their formularies.
The entire process can take years, and according to Hamellin, can result in some companies reaping the benefits of patent exclusivity for fewer than five years in Canada – where developing a single drug can cost $3.5 billion in investment and 10-20 years of research and testing.
Data available through the CDA reveals that fewer than 50 per cent of drugs approved by Health Canada go onto the next stage, limiting its availability through hospitals, private and public insurances.
“Companies make a decision to not submit for reimbursement because it costs money to drive your business for two and a half years before you can actually make that drug available to Canadians,” Hamelin says.
Essentially, Canada doesn’t have a big enough market for some life-saving and life-extending drugs to justify the expense for some pharmaceutical companies. Therefore instead of an “early launch” country Canada becomes a “later launch” country, which delays or even prevents access to innovative new drugs in oncology, organ diseases and non-life ending disorders and diseases.
The federal government created a
Pharmaceutical and Life Sciences task force
last month, which delivered several recommendations on how to streamline the approval process and make Canada more appealing for drug launch. It’s unclear how many of these recommendations will be adopted and how soon. Health Canada did not respond to CityNews’ request by deadline.
“If the recommendations by the task force are implemented, ambitiously, they will help the process, because a number of recommendations address this lengthy sequential process. It calls for doing things more in parallel,“ explains Hamelin.
“We need to look beyond cost to recognise that medicines save lives, save money to the healthcare system, and builds our economy.”
But costs are going to be an ongoing issue particularly because of the U.S. administration’s “most favored nation policy.”
“The side effect of that policy is just going to be that we’re not going to be able to access drugs,” says Hladunewich.
Watch for Part 2 of this multi-part series on Monday on CityNews and citynews.ca.
Ruchi Ambike, who is living with Stage 4 kidney disease is seen with her dog at her home in Mississauga. CITYNEWS

Drugs & Therapies.content:
Semaglutide products, such as Ozempic, are crucial medicines for diabetics, but also popular weight loss drugs. (Photo: DW)
The Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB) has approved seven new semaglutide-based medicines in Kenya, expanding treatment options for people living with type 2 diabetes as demand for the drugs continues to rise.
The approvals follow a regulatory assessment of the medicines' quality, safety, and effectiveness. Although the products contain the same active ingredient, the PPB says they do not necessarily have the same approved uses.
The regulator has also warned the public against using semaglutide medicines without medical supervision, particularly for weight loss.

Semaglutide is a prescription medicine that mimics a natural hormone in the body to help lower blood sugar and reduce appetite. The World Health Organisation (WHO) added the medicine to its Model List of Essential Medicines in September last year.
Kenya previously had two original semaglutide products, Ozempic and Wegovy, both manufactured by Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk. A generic product known as Truglyx was also launched in Nairobi last month during a conference focused on diabetes and obesity.
According to the PPB, Ozempic is approved for adults with type 2 diabetes whose blood sugar is not adequately controlled and should be used alongside diet and physical activity.
Advertisement
Continue reading
The five newly registered generic semaglutide products have also been approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.
Wegovy, however, has a different approved indication. It is authorised for weight management among adults with a high body mass index (BMI), alongside diet and exercise, and can support both initial weight loss and long-term weight management.
PPB Chief Executive Officer Dr Ahmed Mohamed said patients should not assume that different semaglutide products can be substituted for one another simply because they contain the same active ingredient.
“While these products contain the same active ingredient, their approved uses are not necessarily interchangeable and must be understood with reference to the indication approved for each product,” Dr Ahmed said.
The growing popularity of semaglutide, particularly because of its weight-loss effects, has also raised concerns about inappropriate use.
The PPB has previously warned about the increasing off-label and unsupervised use of semaglutide products, especially Ozempic, for weight loss. It is urging members of the public not to use the medicines for self-directed weight loss or buy them from unauthorised sources.
Dr Ahmed said semaglutide medicines are prescription-only and should only be used after assessment and prescription by a qualified healthcare professional.
“Semaglutide-containing medicines are prescription-only medicines and should only be used following appropriate assessment and prescription by a qualified healthcare professional,” he said.
Cost could also affect access to the newly approved medicines. The PPB does not set retail or market prices, but the generic products are reported to cost between Sh13,000 and Sh18,500 per month, while the original products cost between Sh50,000 and Sh75,000 per injection.
The lower price of generic medicines could make semaglutide treatment more accessible to some patients, although the cost may remain high for many Kenyans requiring long-term treatment.
The new approvals come as Kenya continues to face a growing burden of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and obesity. Having more approved medicines could give healthcare providers additional treatment options, but the regulator says appropriate prescribing, monitoring, and patient education remain essential.
For patients, the PPB's message is clear: semaglutide should not be treated as an ordinary weight-loss product. The correct medicine, dose, and indication should be determined by a qualified healthcare professional, and products should be obtained through authorised channels.
The weight-loss drug semaglutide has been associated with several challenges, particularly as its popularity grows among people seeking rapid weight loss. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain, and reduced appetite.
In some cases, severe vomiting or diarrhoea can lead to dehydration and kidney problems. The medicine has also been linked to concerns about pancreatitis and gallbladder problems, making medical supervision important.
Another challenge is that some people may regain weight after stopping treatment, raising questions about the long-term use and affordability of the medicine. In Kenya, cost may also limit access, with generic products still costing thousands of shillings each month.
The growing demand has also raised concerns about people using semaglutide without a prescription or buying it from unauthorised sellers. This increases the risk of inappropriate dosing, side effects, and counterfeit products.
Health experts therefore stress that semaglutide should be prescribed after proper medical assessment and used alongside healthy eating, physical activity, and regular monitoring.
WHO estimates that more than one billion people globally are living with obesity, while about 830 million people have diabetes. The growing demand has also contributed to concerns about shortages, inappropriate use, and falsified semaglutide products being sold through unauthorised channels.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: BMS welcomes new multiple myeloma drug as generics batter current portfolio - BioSpace
Drugs & Therapies.content:
The FDA approves Zenbexus just as copycat competitors depress sales of Bristol Myers Squibb’s multiple myeloma drugs Pomalyst and Revlimid, which crashed 71% and 49% year-on-year, respectively, in the second quarter.
The FDA has granted accelerated approval to Bristol Myers Squibb’s iberdomide for the treatment of multiple myeloma, giving the pharma the opportunity to regain its footing in the indication as generics erode current sales.
Iberdomide, now to carry the brand name Zenbexus, is indicated as part of a treatment regimen with dexamethasone and Johnson & Johnson’s Darzalex for patients who have undergone at least one prior line of treatment, according to a
news release on Thursday
. The drug carries a
boxed warning
for embryo-fetal toxicity and serious venous and arterial thromboembolism.
For full and continued approval, BMS will need to verify the clinical benefit of Zenbexus in a late-stage confirmatory study.
Zenbexus costs $29,500 for a 28-day cycle, higher than what analysts at William Blair had initially expected, according to a Friday morning note. The firm expects the drug to go over $1 billion in annual earnings by 2031.
The approval of Zenbexus comes amid declining sales of BMS’ other multiple myeloma drugs. Revlimid, first approved in 2005,
crashed 49% year-on-year
to make $425 million worldwide in the second quarter. Meanwhile, Pomalyst, generics for which entered the market
earlier this year
, plummeted 71% to $204 million worldwide in Q2.
BMS has been managing the erosion of these products well, however, clocking
$12.97 billion
in total revenue for the second quarter—a 5% year-on-year increase and a comfortable beat over the $11.73 billion consensus. The company has lifted 2026 sales guidance by 6% to $49.5 billion.
Earnings
BMS’ ‘big beat’ clouded by Cobenfy, heart disease data delays
Strong quarterly results are prompting Bristol Myers Squibb to lift its 2026 outlook, though the company is facing another delay for key Cobenfy Alzheimer’s data and a pushed-back readout for milvexian.
July 30, 2026
·
4 min read
·
Gabrielle Masson
Read more
The FDA’s verdict on Thursday was supported by data from the Phase 3 EXCALIBER-RRMM study, which found that the Zenbexus-based regimen elicited a significantly higher rate of minimal residual disease (MRD)-negative complete response than standard of care. MRD negativity is considered a predictor of progression-free survival, BMS said.
Zenbexus is the first approval for BMS’s
CELMoD platform
, which makes use of cells’ innate trash disposal system to target and destroy abnormal proteins that would otherwise lead to cancer. Another CELMoD candidate called mezigdomide is also under FDA review for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, with a
decision due next May
.
BMS recently made headlines earlier this month when
The Financial Times
reported that the pharma was in talks with AstraZeneca for a potential mega-merger. Given their respective sizes and overlapping portfolios, many analysts
dismissed the deal as “unlikely.”
Indeed, just days later, an anonymous source with knowledge of the matter
disavowed the rumor
, telling
Reuters
that “there never was a deal to be done, and there are no discussions between the companies.”

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: ArkBio's RSV Antiviral Drug Ziresovir Receives FDA Approval for Phase II Clinical Trial - PR Newswire
Drugs & Therapies.content:
SHANGHAI
,
Aug. 14, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- Shanghai Ark Biopharmaceutical Co., Ltd. ("ArkBio") today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved ziresovir (AK0529) for a phase II clinical trial in the severely ill RSV infected infant patients, including the ones in pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).
Severe RSV Infection: An Urgent Unmet Need in PICU
RSV is the leading pathogen of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) in infants and young children globally, causing approximately 33 million LRTI cases, 3.6 million hospitalizations, and more than 100,000 deaths annually. Severely ill RSV infected infants often require admission to the PICU for intensive care such as respiratory support, with rapid disease progression, high risk and a heavy medical burden. There is currently no approved RSV-specific antiviral therapy worldwide; clinical management remains limited to symptomatic and supportive care, such as oxygenation, leaving an urgent unmet need for effective antiviral treatment in hospitalized RSV infected patients with severe diseases.
Ziresovir Advances to Treat Severely Infected Infant Patients
Ziresovir is the first direct RSV antiviral drug to successfully complete a phase III clinical trial with positive results. The clinical study in 1-24 months age patients conducted in China demonstrated that ziresovir can significantly reduce viral load, accelerate the resolution of respiratory symptoms, and significantly lower the risk of recurrent wheezing and asthma over 24-month follow-up period, with a favorable safety profile. Key findings from the clinical study have been published in
The New England Journal of Medicine
and
The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health
. In 2025, ziresovir was included as the only therapeutic drug in the WHO's Paediatric Drug Optimization for Respiratory Syncytial Virus publication. The newly approved phase II clinical trial marks the extension of ziresovir's clinical development into the most critically ill RSV patients, representing a key milestone in the clinical development of ziresovir globally.
FDA Approved Phase II Clinical Trial
The approved multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial will focus on severely ill RSV infected infants requiring hospitalization in PICU, one of the most critical RSV patient populations with the most urgent clinical treatment needs. This clinical trial is designed to evaluate clinical efficacy of ziresovir, especially the length of oxygen treatment and sustained recovery time, providing the clinical basis for the future registrational trials.
About ArkBio
ArkBio is a commercial-stage biotechnology company focused on the discovery and development of innovative therapeutics for respiratory/lung and pediatric diseases. Founded in 2014, the company has established proprietary technology platforms and a differentiated R&D pipeline through internal innovation and strategic collaborations.
Key pipeline assets include: ziresovir (AK0529), the first direct-acting antiviral for RSV with positive phase 3 results; AK3280, a potentially best-in-class anti-fibrotic agent with positive phase 2 results in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, currently in phase 3 registrational trials; AK0901, approved and commercialized in China for ADHD treatment. The company also has multiple first-in-class or best-in-class innovative drug candidates in clinical or preclinical development.
ArkBio has established strategic partnerships with multinational pharmaceutical companies including Roche and Genentech, leading academic institutions including The Scripps Research Institute and the Institute of Microbiology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Qilu Pharmaceutical, as well as other domestic and international biotech companies and CROs.
For more information, please visit:
www.arkbiosciences.com

[email protected]

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Heavy R&D investment, strong policy support, and global cooperation drive rapid growth of China's innovative drug industry - Global Times
Drugs & Therapies.content:
A worker operates a machine at a pharmaceutical company in Yanji, Northeast China's Jilin Province on August 11, 2026. Photo: VCG
"In the past, Chinese people used to believe that imported drugs were better than domestically made. Now, European and American markets are pinning hope on Chinese innovative drugs to cure their patients," said Liu Daogang, Party chief of the Tianjin International Joint Academy of Biotechnology & Medicine, commenting on a tectonic shift in how people around the world view Chinese-made drugs.
"This represents the emergence of Chinese innovative drugs after years of development, reflecting the advantages of China's national system and R&D strength, which marked the arrival of  a 'DeepSeek moment' for China-made biopharmaceuticals," Liu told the Global Times on Friday. Hisinstitution has helped incubate listed companies such as CanSino Biotech and Danna Biotech.
In recent years, China's innovative pharmaceutical sector has gained global influence, with outbound technology licensing transactions reaching $110 billion in the first six months of 2026. In the first half, Chinese companies signed 81 outbound licensing agreements for innovative drugs with partners in 20 countries and regions, including the US, Britain, France and Italy. The total deal value reached 80 percent of the full-year figure for 2025.
China's innovative pharmaceutical sector has reached its "DeepSeek moment," the point at which years of sustained investment in infrastructure and regulatory framework are beginning to deliver tangible breakthroughs, industry insiders told the Global Times.
The global expansion of Chinese pharmaceutical companies has moved from the shallow waters of "product going global" to the deep waters of "value co-creation," while the rapid progress of Chinese innovative drugs is delivering new solutions to patients around the world, the insiders said.
Chinese innovation
Multinationals have in recent years stepped up cooperation with Chinese drug-makers, with some leading figures in the industry acknowledging that China has evolved from a "follower" into a "source" of original biopharmaceutical innovation.
Lan Gongtao, an official with the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), said in January that China's outbound licensing transaction value in 2025 doubled from the previous year, while the number of approved innovative drugs also hit a record high, as a result of deepening drug review and approval reforms and the government's pro-innovation policies, the CCTV News reported.
While the number of innovative drugs has grown, China has maintained high standards aligned with international norms, and the surge in outbound licensing reflected international recognition of the value of Chinese innovative drugs, Lan said.
Jin Lei, founder and chief scientist of GeneScience Pharmaceutical Co Ltd, said that as more Chinese products and services are exported to other parts of the world, quality drugs from China are set to benefit more patients globally.
In 2025, GenSci signed its first overseas business development licensing deal worth up to $1.365 billion. The candidate is designed to directly disrupt the central mechanism of both Graves' disease (GD) and thyroid eye disease (TED), and GenSci's breakthrough offers hope to tens of millions of patients worldwide. "This is a direct response of Chinese wisdom," said Jin.
According to a post seen on the company's website, it recorded a three-year average growth rate of 164 percent in the global market, while its overseas revenue exceeded 100 million yuan, with its products reaching nearly 40 markets in Latin America, Southeast Asia, Middle East and North Africa. This significantly improves access to high-quality Chinese biologics, while providing advanced treatment options at affordable costs, improving local health conditions, Jin said.
According to Pharmcube, a pharmaceutical industry consultancy, China surpassed the US in the number of original drugs developed between 2015 and 2024, cementing its place among the world's leading innovators in pharmaceuticals, Xinhua News Agency reported. During that decade, the cumulative value of overseas licensing deals involving Chinese innovative drugs exceeded $1.2 trillion. Eighteen China-developed original medicines were approved abroad, with several outperforming foreign origin drugs in head-to-head clinical trials.
'Made in China' strength
These results highlight the transformation of China's pharmaceutical sector, which was once dominated by generic and imitative medicines.
China's domestic pharmaceutical industry is gradually moving away from imitative drug development, forming a new landscape in which artificial intelligence (AI) empowers front-end research and development (R&D), local enterprises drive independent innovation, and high-quality products reach global markets, demonstrating the vitality of new quality productive forces, analysts said.
In a sense, the success of Chinese innovative drugs is an extension of the success of China's overall manufacturing sector.
Policy support has played its role too. In the country's outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), the government designated the biopharmaceutical industry as a strategic development sector.
Noting the progress achieved by China's innovative drugs in recent years, Liu said China has moved from following to running alongside the world's most advanced drugmakers, while taking the lead in some areas.
Regulators have continuously optimized policies and aligned with international standards to establish review and inspection systems with Chinese characteristics, greatly shortening approval timelines, Liu said.
Moreover, China's large population creates strong demand for treatments for complex and chronic diseases, laying a foundation for innovative drug R&D. Emerging technologies such as AI and supercomputing have strengthened the biopharma industry, enabling Chinese companies to catch up with and even surpass their European and American counterparts in the race to develop new drugs, Liu said.
Samuel Zhang, CBO of Suzhou-based biopharmaceutical company Innovent Biologics, told the Global Times on Thursday that the accelerated global expansion of Chinese innovative drugs is linked to new business models that emphasize co-development and benefit-sharing.
In 2025, Innovent Biologics inked several major deals with global pharmaceutical giants, involving deeper and more reciprocal cooperation, including co-development and co-commercialization in overseas markets.
"For instance, in May, in a partnership with a leading US pharmaceutical company, we agreed to engage in co-developing some of the key projects globally, and share the risks together. If the endeavor is proved successful, we will share the profits," Zhang said.
This new collaboration model has set a benchmark for the high-quality global expansion of Chinese innovative drugs and Chinese pharmaceutical companies, significantly enhancing their global influence, Zhang said.
Liu noted that another advantage comes from China's approach to drug pipeline development. At the national level, the government issues annual guidelines on major new drug development, which help chart the direction for drug research and development.
Strengthened regulatory oversight has also played an important role. China's drug regulatory system reform, launched in 2015, has introduced fast-track pathways for a set of breakthrough therapies, conditional approvals, and priority reviews, effectively shortening timelines across the drug development cycle.
"In recent years, the national guidance has focused on curing a series of complex chronic diseases, including infectious diseases, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases. Such top-level design helps pharmaceutical companies avoid detours and stay on target," Liu said.

Zurich: Drugmakers are holding back applications for health insurance ​coverage in Switzerland over concerns ​that lower prices there could affect their U.S. business ​under drug-pricing policies introduced by the Trump administration, a study showed on Thursday.
About one-third of new
innovative medicines
were not submitted for coverage under Switzerland's mandatory health insurance system ‌between January ⁠2025 and ⁠June 2026, according to a survey by Swiss pharmaceutical industry group Interpharma, potentially limiting patient access to new treatments.
Switzerland is one of the countries used as a benchmark under ​the United States' so-called most-favoured-nation drug-pricing policy, which aims to lower U.S. medicine costs by comparing prices with those in other markets.
Advt
The policy has ​made some drugmakers more hesitant about launching new ⁠medicines in ‌Europe for fear of undermining U.S. pricing.
"The survey shows ​drug makers ​no longer consider themselves able to launch new therapies ⁠in Switzerland in a timely manner under the current framework ​conditions, so as not to jeopardize prices in the ​United States," Interpharma said.
The survey found that seven of 22 new innovative drugs introduced during the period were not submitted for inclusion on Switzerland's reimbursement list, which determines whether drugs are covered by mandatory health insurance and sets the reimbursed price.
Another three were not submitted for Swiss ‌market approval at all, which Interpharma also attributed to the U.S. most-favoured-nation policy.
While companies such as Roche and Novartis may still ​launch medicines ​in Switzerland, inclusion ⁠on the reimbursement list is important for broad patient access and establishes a price that could influence U.S. comparisons.
The 15 medicines submitted for reimbursement compared ​with an average of 24 submissions over the same 18-month period between 2019 and 2025, Interpharma said.
As a result, Swiss patients do not have access to about one-third of newly developed innovative medicines through mandatory health insurance, with the U.S. policy exacerbating an existing trend, the group said.
Advt
(Reporting by Marleen Kaesebier in Zurich. Editing by Mark Potter)

Drugs & Therapies.content:
By
Benjamin Eddie
Published: Aug 14 2026, 4:49 PM EDT
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter

Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard
Share on Pocket
James Yarema/unsplash.com
Eighteen months after the FDA told Takeda Pharmaceutical that its soticlestat data package could not support a drug application, the first-in-class CH24H inhibitor has a new owner and a new clinical bet. Ovid Therapeutics and Takeda have
transferred global IP rights for soticlestat
— a novel oral therapy targeting a brain enzyme unlike any approved epilepsy drug — to a new privately held company launched by specialist biotech investor Perceptive Advisors. The deal, disclosed as part of Ovid's second-quarter 2026 financial results, represents a calculated gamble that what failed was not soticlestat's underlying mechanism but the specific trial design that was used to test it.
For the approximately
48,000 Americans with LGS
and the estimated 15,000 to 25,000 with Dravet syndrome — conditions in which roughly 90 percent of patients cannot achieve adequate seizure control on existing medications — the revival of soticlestat matters because it is the only drug in clinical development that works through CH24H inhibition, a pharmacological approach never before validated in any approved therapy.
What CH24H Inhibition Is and Why It Matters
Soticlestat targets an enzyme called cholesterol 24-hydroxylase — also designated CYP46A1 — that
exists almost exclusively in the brain
. Under normal conditions, CYP46A1 converts cholesterol into 24S-hydroxycholesterol (24HC) as part of the brain's mechanism for managing its cholesterol load. The problem is that 24HC is not biologically inert once produced: it acts as a positive allosteric modulator of NMDA receptors — the same class of glutamate receptors involved in excitatory signaling — and can compound the problem by
impairing glutamate clearance from synapses
, the transport mechanism responsible for clearing glutamate from the synaptic cleft. The net result, under conditions where CYP46A1 becomes overactive, is a vicious cycle: more 24HC produces more NMDA receptor activation, which produces more glutamate release, which is then cleared more slowly, producing more neuronal overexcitation and more seizures.
By blocking CYP46A1, soticlestat interrupts this cycle at the source. A 2025 review in the journal Epilepsia by Kondo and colleagues identified
three distinct antiseizure mechanisms
that the drug may operate through: reduction of 24HC-mediated NMDA receptor overactivation, restoration of glutamate clearance from the synaptic cleft, and suppression of neuroinflammatory signaling through a TNF-alpha-dependent pathway. Notably, the same review acknowledged that the exact mechanism "remains undetermined" and that the three pathways represent a "working hypothesis" rather than an established fact — a scientific gap that the Perceptive NewCo will need to resolve.
None of the three approved drugs for Dravet syndrome — stiripentol, cannabidiol (marketed as Epidiolex), and fenfluramine (marketed as Fintepla) — works through any of these pathways. Stiripentol modulates sodium channels and enhances GABA inhibitory signaling; cannabidiol acts through multiple mechanisms including transient receptor potential channels; fenfluramine is primarily a serotonin 2C receptor agonist. Soticlestat, if validated, would represent a pharmacologically independent class — not an add-on to existing mechanisms but a new one. That remains the core of the scientific argument for giving it another chance.
How the First Attempt Ended
Soticlestat's original development journey spanned nearly a decade. Discovered at Takeda's research center in Shonan, Japan, it was
developed in collaboration with Ovid Therapeutics
beginning in 2017, with the partnership expanded the following year. In 2021, Takeda assumed full development and commercial rights in a transaction that included
an upfront payment to Ovid
of approximately $196 million and the potential for up to $660 million in additional milestones.
A Phase 2 study called ELEKTRA had produced encouraging results, showing a
statistically significant seizure frequency reduction
compared with placebo in a combined Dravet and LGS population, with particularly strong results in the Dravet cohort. Those results funded two large, registrational Phase 3 programs: SKYLINE in Dravet syndrome and SKYWAY in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
The
Phase 3 readout in June 2024
was a setback significant enough to immediately reshape Ovid's future. In SKYLINE, the primary endpoint — reduction from baseline in convulsive seizure frequency compared with placebo over 16 weeks — was narrowly missed, with a p-value of 0.06 against the conventional 0.05 threshold. In SKYWAY, soticlestat
missed its primary endpoint
of reducing major motor drop seizures in LGS patients.
What the headline numbers did not fully convey was the secondary-endpoint picture. In SKYLINE, six of six key secondary endpoints — the responder rate, clinician and caregiver global impressions of improvement, and measures of seizure intensity and duration — all showed clinically meaningful, nominally significant results, each with
p-values at or below 0.008
. Takeda recorded a full impairment loss of JPY 21.5 billion on soticlestat's intangible assets in its quarter ending June 30, 2024, based on those trial outcomes.
Takeda subsequently engaged the FDA to assess whether the totality of evidence could support a new drug application. The answer, relayed in January 2025, was that it could not: the FDA told Takeda that the
existing data package was insufficient
for NDA approval in Dravet syndrome. The LGS program had already been wound down. Takeda formally discontinued the entire soticlestat program on January 30, 2025.
Why Perceptive Is Willing to Try Again
The scientific argument for a renewed attempt centers on three observations.
First, the FDA's rejection was explicitly addressed to the existing data package, not to soticlestat's mechanism of action. Takeda's January 2025 statement uses careful language: "the current clinical data package would not be capable of demonstrating substantial evidence of effectiveness." That formulation leaves room for a new data package generated by a differently designed trial. No approved drug exists that targets CYP46A1, meaning the mechanism itself has never been invalidated — only the specific trial that attempted to prove it.
Second, the SKYLINE near-miss (p=0.06) is genuinely unusual. A drug that misses a primary endpoint while producing consistent, significant secondary effects across five additional measures is not a drug that does nothing. In rare pediatric epilepsy, where trial design challenges are well-documented and placebo effects can be pronounced, advocates for soticlestat have argued that a different primary endpoint, a longer treatment window beyond the 16-week assessment period used in SKYLINE, or an enrichment strategy targeting patient subgroups more likely to show the
primary-endpoint benefit
could produce a different result. The 2026 SKYWAY full results paper in Epilepsia by Guerrini and colleagues also showed
nominally significant secondary outcomes
on clinical global impression scales (p=0.032 and p=0.029), suggesting a signal even in the more clearly negative LGS trial.
Third, the regulatory incentives attached to soticlestat remain intact. It holds both Orphan Drug Designation — providing seven-year market exclusivity upon approval, tax credits for clinical trial costs, and reduced FDA fees — and Rare Pediatric Disease Designation. The Rare Pediatric Disease Designation is particularly meaningful: a successful NDA could yield a transferable Priority Review Voucher, which in recent years has commanded $100 million or more on the secondary market and represents a standalone financial incentive independent of the drug's commercial potential.
Perceptive Advisors, founded in New York in 1999 by Joseph Edelman, has built its reputation on exactly this kind of bet — deep scientific due diligence in small- and mid-cap biotech, with a track record of backing both public crossover rounds and
focused private biotech vehicles
. The NewCo structure — a focused, independently capitalized vehicle with no obligation to compete against a parent company's other pipeline assets — may be better positioned than Takeda or Ovid to pursue the patient subgroup analysis, endpoint redesign, or alternative indication work that the existing data suggests could be fruitful.
What the Deal Means for Ovid
For Ovid Therapeutics, the transaction is financially elegant. The company, which had been operationally built around the Takeda collaboration and used the 2021 upfront payment to fund its independent pipeline, now holds an equity stake in the NewCo along with the right to collect
up to $294.5 million in potential milestones
if soticlestat reaches approval and sales targets. A portion of those milestones is payable to Ligand Pharmaceuticals under a previously disclosed royalty monetization agreement through which Ovid had sold a minority interest in soticlestat economics to extend its own cash runway. Low- to mid-single-digit royalties on net sales are also possible if the drug is commercialized.
As Ovid CEO Meg Alexander noted in the Q2 statement, the arrangement gives the company the potential to "realize value from our interests in soticlestat, which may provide future capital to Ovid and, most importantly, advance a meaningful therapy to epilepsy patients who can benefit." Ovid held $169.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities as of June 30, 2026, with
financial runway projected into 2029
.
Ovid's own pipeline has moved substantially beyond the soticlestat era. The company is advancing OV4071 — described as the first-ever oral direct activator of the potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 (KCC2) transporter, a mechanism relevant to excitatory/inhibitory balance across dozens of central nervous system disease models — through an ongoing Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, with data intended to support a Phase 2 proof-of-concept study in acute schizophrenia in 2027. OV329, a next-generation GABA-aminotransferase inhibitor, has entered Phase 2 proof-of-concept studies in treatment-resistant focal onset seizures and tuberous sclerosis complex.
Does This Bet Make Scientific Sense?
The honest answer is: it might.
The scientific case is real, not merely promotional. The CH24H/CYP46A1 pathway is genuinely implicated in neuronal hyperexcitability through mechanisms that existing approved drugs do not address. The p=0.06 SKYLINE primary-endpoint miss, combined with uniformly
significant secondary outcomes at p=0.008
, is not a pattern that drug development investors typically see in compounds that do nothing — it is more consistent with a drug whose benefit is real but whose primary-endpoint measure failed to fully capture it in the specific study population and time frame used.
The cautionary notes are equally real. A 2026 structure-activity relationship study in the journal Molecules noted that soticlestat suffers from
"unsatisfactory in vivo potency"
in animal models and clinical trials — a concern that any redesigned trial program will need to confront. The FDA's explicit statement that the existing data cannot support an NDA is a high barrier. And drug development in rare pediatric epilepsy has frustrated many programs whose preclinical signals were compelling.
What the Perceptive NewCo is betting is not simply that soticlestat works — but that the way it was tested was the problem. That is a scientifically defensible position. Whether it is correct will depend on how creatively and rigorously the new team can reimagine the clinical question the drug is being asked to answer.
For patients with Dravet syndrome and related epileptic encephalopathies — who have lived through the rise and fall of soticlestat's first development arc — this revival offers a cautious reason for renewed attention, alongside the reminder that no drug in rare pediatric epilepsy has ever had an easy path.
Currency conversion note: the JPY 21.5 billion write-down figure is expressed as approximately $135 million USD based on the exchange rate on August 14, 2026; currency conversions are approximate.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is soticlestat and how is it different from existing epilepsy drugs?
Soticlestat is an oral inhibitor of cholesterol 24-hydroxylase (CYP46A1), a brain-specific enzyme that converts cholesterol into a molecule called 24S-hydroxycholesterol (24HC). Excess 24HC amplifies neuronal firing by stimulating NMDA glutamate receptors and impairing the clearance of glutamate from the synaptic cleft — a dual mechanism that drives the overexcitability underlying certain severe seizure disorders. Every drug currently approved for Dravet syndrome works through a completely different mechanism: stiripentol through sodium channels and GABA signaling, cannabidiol through multiple pathways including TRP channels, and fenfluramine through serotonin receptors. Soticlestat, if validated, would be the first approved drug to target the CYP46A1 pathway — an entirely separate pharmacological class.
Why did soticlestat fail in Phase 3, and why does Perceptive think a new attempt could succeed?
Soticlestat's SKYLINE Phase 3 trial in Dravet syndrome missed its primary endpoint — reduction in convulsive seizure frequency — by a very narrow margin, with a p-value of 0.06 against the conventional 0.05 threshold. At the same time, all six key secondary endpoints, including clinician and caregiver global impressions of improvement and measures of seizure intensity and duration, were statistically significant at p=0.008 or better. The FDA told Takeda that the existing data package could not support a new drug application — but that language referred to the specific data already collected, not to the drug's mechanism. Perceptive's bet is that a redesigned trial — potentially with a different primary endpoint, a longer treatment window, or an enriched patient population — could generate a data package that tells a more convincing story to regulators.
What does "first-in-class mechanism" actually mean for patients, and is an approval realistic?
First-in-class means soticlestat is the first drug to target the CYP46A1/24HC pathway in a clinical setting — no other approved drug has ever validated this mechanism. For patients who have already tried all three approved Dravet drugs and still have frequent, uncontrolled seizures (which describes the majority of the patient population), a new mechanism is not merely a convenience — it represents access to a completely different biological lever. Whether approval is realistic depends on what clinical strategy the Perceptive NewCo pursues. The barriers are substantial: the FDA has already reviewed the full SKYLINE/SKYWAY dataset and found it insufficient. A new approval attempt would almost certainly require new clinical trial data, not reanalysis of existing trials.
What financial incentives does the NewCo have beyond commercial drug sales?
Beyond potential royalties and milestone payments to Ovid, soticlestat's Rare Pediatric Disease Designation from the FDA means that a successful new drug application could generate a Priority Review Voucher — a transferable regulatory document that allows the holder to receive expedited FDA review of any drug of their choosing. These vouchers have sold on the secondary market for $100 million or more in recent years, representing a standalone financial incentive for the NewCo that is entirely separate from soticlestat's commercial prospects in the epilepsy market.
